newsitem.title: USA: Bitter Koch family feud set for trial in 1998.
newsitem.headline: Bitter Koch family feud set for trial in 1998.

text.p: A bitter family feud between members of the wealthy Koch family looks set to go to trial in 1998 following a ruling by a federal district court judge in Kansas, a lawyer for the plaintiffs said Wednesday.

"I think chances of a settlement now are remote," said trial lawyer Don Scott of Bartlit Beck, the Chicago firm acting for the plaintiffs, William and Frederick Koch and the Simmons, Koch family cousins.

The dispute goes back to 1983 when the plaintiffs agreed to sell out their interests in Koch Industries for $1.1 billion after falling out with Charles Koch, chairman and chief executive officer of the Wichita, Kan.-based company, the second-largest privately-held firm in the United States.
Charles is the brother of William and Frederick Koch.
Judge Sam Crow last Friday ruled that the plaintiffs could persue three of 12 claims against Charles, another brother David, Koch Industries and other Koch executives.
The substance of the claims is that Charles and Koch Industries withheld information which they were legally required to disclose, leading to an undervaluation of the plaintiffs' shares, Scott said.
Koch Industries, in a statement Tuesday evening, characterized the judge's ruling as a victory.
"The court ruled that, as a matter of law, there is no basis for 75 percent of William Koch's claims," said Don Cordes, a Koch Industries executive vice president, in the statement.
But Judge Crow allowed three claims to proceed which account for about two-thirds of the plantiffs' monetary claim, Scott argued.

"Our claim is still for over $300 million of actual damages as of June 1983, on top of which there is 15 years of pre-judgement interest and punitive damages in an amount to be determined," said Scott. He said the claim would be for well over $1 billion.

Judge Crow heard the plaintiffs claim that Charles knew two days before the share sale agreement was signed of a deal that would prove "a watershed event in the company's fortunes," substantially boosting the market for the company's oil refinery in Minnesota, said Scott.
Other claims center on whether Koch broke disclosure rules in accounting for its 1982 earnings, a key factor in valuing the plaintiffs' shares.
Koch Industries representatives didn't return phone calls Wednesday.
"We look forward to a trial on the remaining issues and are confident that we will prevail when all is said and done," said Cordes, the Koch executive, in Tuesday's statement.
A trial is expected in spring or early summer 1998, to be held in federal court in either Wichita or Topeka, Scott said.
